enonce_markdown: A stack is initially empty. The operations push(5), push(8), push(2), pop(), pop() are carried out in this order. Which value is now on top of the stack?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure: push adds to the top and pop removes the item that was added most recently.

### Solution

After the three pushes the stack holds 5, 8, 2 (2 on top). The first pop removes 2, the second removes 8, leaving only 5. The top is **5** (a simulation gives the same). Option a is the first value removed, and option c is the second.

enonce_markdown: Customers at a bank in Douala are served strictly in the order in which they arrive. Which abstract data type models this behaviour best?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO): items are added at the rear (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue).

### Solution

Serving customers in order of arrival is FIFO behaviour, so the model is a **queue**. A stack would serve the latest arrival first. A binary tree and an array are not defined by an arrival-order rule; an array is also a concrete data structure rather than an abstract data type.

enonce_markdown: A queue is initially empty. The operations enqueue(4), enqueue(7), enqueue(1), dequeue(), enqueue(9), dequeue() are performed in order. What does a call to front() (which returns the first item without removing it) return now?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Dequeue removes the oldest item, from the front; enqueue adds at the rear. Track the queue after every operation.

### Solution

| Operation | Queue (front on the left) |
|---|---|
| enqueue 4, 7, 1 | 4, 7, 1 |
| dequeue (removes 4) | 7, 1 |
| enqueue 9 | 7, 1, 9 |
| dequeue (removes 7) | 1, 9 |

The front is **1**. Option b is the first item removed and option c the second; option d is the last item added (a stack-like reading).

enonce_markdown: A team in Bamenda implements a Stack ADT with an array. Later they change the implementation to a linked list, and none of the programs that call push, pop and peek has to be modified. Which feature of abstract data types makes this possible?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

An ADT is defined by its operations (its interface) and not by the way they are coded. Users depend only on the interface, so the implementation stays hidden and can be replaced.

### Solution

Programs only use push, pop and peek, which form the interface. The array or linked list is hidden behind it, so replacing it does not affect the callers. The correct answer is the **separation of the interface from the implementation (information hiding)**. Inheritance relates classes to each other, iteration is a way of repeating instructions, and data redundancy is the unwanted duplication of data in a database.

choix.texte: Separation of the interface from the implementation (information hiding)

(a) List four operations of a Stack abstract data type and state what each one does. (4 marks)

(b) State a precondition for the operation pop and say what should happen if it is not met. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why a programmer who uses a Stack does not need to know whether it is stored in an array or in a linked list. (2 marks)

A postfix (reverse Polish) expression is evaluated with a stack: each number is pushed; each operator pops two values, applies the operator and pushes the result. The second value popped is the left operand. What is the value of the expression `6 2 3 + * 4 -`?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Scan left to right. For an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left operand, compute left (operator) right and push the result back.

### Solution

| Token | Action | Stack (top on the right) |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | push | 6 |
| 2 | push | 6, 2 |
| 3 | push | 6, 2, 3 |
| + | 2 + 3 = 5 | 6, 5 |
| * | 6 * 5 = 30 | 30 |
| 4 | push | 30, 4 |
| - | 30 - 4 = 26 | 26 |

The value is **26** (confirmed by a short program). The expression is (6 x (2 + 3)) - 4. Option b results from computing 6 x 2 + 3 - 4; option c from computing (6 + 2) x 3 - 4; option a from reversing the operands of the last subtraction (4 - 30).
